$comment: The server-components wire format, and the two decoders that read it.
`encodeFlightPayload` in packages/ruvyxa/runtime/flight.mjs writes every
payload -- for `/__ruvyxa/flight`, for `POST /__ruvyxa/rsc`, and for the
error envelope `publicFlightError` produces. Two things read one back:
- decodeFlightPayload, beside the encoder in flight.mjs
- decodeFlight in packages/@ruvyxa/react/src/router.ts
The second is the one that runs. Nothing in this repository calls the
first outside its own unit test, and nothing at all called the second: the
decoder every browser executes on every soft navigation into a
server-components route had no test, while the round-trip test beside the
encoder made the format look covered. A change to the encoder and its
sibling decoder would have stayed green and broken every browser, and the
symptom is not an error anybody sees -- `startFlight` rejects, the router
falls back to `hardNavigate`, and a soft navigation quietly becomes a full
page load.
The three limits were the same shape. `MAX_NODES` and `MAX_DEPTH` in
flight.mjs against bare `10_000` and `64` inside `assertFlightValue`, and
`DEFAULT_FLIGHT_LIMIT` against `FLIGHT_BYTE_LIMIT` -- one number per pair,
two spellings, and both halves in JavaScript, which is outside
scripts/check-cross-language-constants.mjs entirely: it enumerates names
declared in *both languages*, so a JavaScript-to-JavaScript pair is never
compared.
Both decoders replay `cases` below:
- tests/packages/ruvyxa/flight.test.mjs
- packages/@ruvyxa/react/test/flight-decoder.test.mjs
$limitsComment: `byteLimit` is enforced by the browser alone, before it decodes: the
encoder has no size bound, because the thing that produces an oversize
payload is a route rendering more data than a navigation should carry, and
refusing it at encode time would fail the page rather than the
optimisation. Recorded here so the two numbers cannot drift apart -- the
server producing what the browser refuses is a permanent hard navigation
for that route with nothing in any log.
$casesComment: `tree` is the value under test. `accept: false` means both decoders must
refuse the payload; the message is deliberately not compared, because the
two report in different registers -- RUV1830 for the framework's own
diagnostic channel, a plain Error for the browser's.
`build` names a shape a JSON literal cannot express, so each host
constructs it. Each bound is covered from both sides, because only one of
the two directions is visible from either alone: `atDepth`/`atNodes` sit
exactly on the limit and must be accepted, which is what catches a
decoder that *narrowed* its bound below what the encoder writes, and
`deep`/`wide` sit one step past it and must be refused, which catches one
that dropped the check. A limit that only ever fails from above passes
just as happily at half its value.
